The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION], [ LOCATION]. He was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed burglary. He was charged with two counts of burglary and detained on remand in view of the reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. He lodged a complaint with the Biała Podlaska District Court, maintaining that his detention was unlawful because the detention order had been made by the prosecutor, who did not have the attributes of a “judge” required under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. The court deemed the complaint to be an appeal against the detentionorder of [Date_TIME]. It examined it as such and dismissed it.

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION], [ LOCATION]. He was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed burglary. He was charged with two counts of burglary and detained on remand. The court considered that the applicant should be detained because there was a reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. The applicant complained to the Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor and the Ombudsman that, after having been arrested, he had not been brought before a judge but before the prosecutor, who was not authorised by law to exercise judicial power. The application was dismissed and the applicant convicted of dealing with stolen goods.

The applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed burglary. He was charged with two counts of burglary and detained on remand in view of the reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. He lodged a complaint with the Biała Podlaska District Court, maintaining that his detention was unlawful. The court deemed the complaint to be an appeal against the detention order of [DATE_TIME]. It examined it as such and dismissed it on [Date_TIME] The court gave judgment and convicted the applicant of dealing with stolen goods. The applicant appealed against his conviction to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court replied to the applicant's complaint in the following way: “ ... Under Article 210 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a court imposes preventive measures after a bill of indictment has been lodged with that court; beforehand - a prosecutor [imposes such measures]. It thus follows that your doubts as to the imposition of detention [in your case] are unreasonable. ...” The case was referred to the Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor. He was not brought before a judge but before the district prosecutor, the Supreme Court said. The application was dismissed without prejudice to the court's previous rulings on the case.

The Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor had brought the case before a judge, rather than a court. The Supreme Court replied to the applicant's complaint in the following way: “ ... Under Article 210 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a court imposes preventive measures after a bill of indictment has been lodged with that court. ...” “It thus follows that your doubts as to the imposition of detention [in your case] are unreasonable,” the Supreme Court said. “Everyone detained shall be brought promptly before a. judge – or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power. Under [the relevant] legislation, a prosecutor is such an officer. ...

The applicant complained that he had not been brought before a judge but before the Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor. The Case-law Department of the Supreme Court replied to the applicant's complaint in the following way: “ ... Under Article 210 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a court imposes preventive measures after a bill of indictment has been lodged with that court; beforehand - a prosecutor [imposes such measures]. It thus follows that your doubts as to the imposition of detention [in your case] are unreasonable. ...’’ The application was rejected on the grounds that the prosecutor had not carried out his duties under the relevant legislation.

The owner of real property filed a civil action for damages against the tenant. On [DATE_TIME] her action was dismissed by a judgment of the Zielona Góra Regional Court. The applicant appealed against the judgment. Her cassation appeal was rejected by a decision of the Poznań Court of Appeal. The appellant lodged an appeal with the Supreme Court against the decision of that panel. Judge [PERSON] presided over the panel which gave this decision and also acted as the judge rapporteur on the admissibility issue. The court held that the appeal did not comply with a procedural requirement set out in Article 393 3 § 1 (3) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The owner of real property filed a civil action for damages against the tenant. Her action was dismissed by a judgment of the Zielona Góra Regional Court. The applicant appealed against the judgment. On [DATE_TIME] her appeal was rejected by a decision of the Poznań Court of Appeal. She then lodged an appeal with the Supreme Court against the decision of that panel. She argued that the fact that the same judge had sat on a panel giving a second-instance judgment on the merits and subsequently rejecting a cassation appeal against that judgment rendered the proceedings unfair. The Supreme Court ruled that the appeal did not comply with a procedural requirement.

The owner of real property which she had been renting filed a civil action for damages against the tenant. On [DATE_TIME] her action was dismissed by a judgment of the Zielona Góra Regional Court. The applicant appealed against the judgment through a panel of the Poznań Court of Appeal. Her cassation appeal was rejected by a decision of that panel. The court noted the case-law of the Supreme Court on the interpretation of Article 393 3 § 1 (3) of the Code. The mere fact that the appeal contained arguments to show the grounds on which it had been lodged was insufficient for the appeal to be declared admissible.

The judge could refuse to entertain a cassation appeal if it considered that no significant legal issue arose in the case. It referred to the applicant’s objection in one sentence only: “The fact that the judge, who took part in the judgment against which the appeal was subsequently lodged, participated in a decision by which this appeal was found inadmissible is of no significance” The judge ruled that the appeal should be rejected. The appeal was dismissed as ‘inadmissible’ and the case was thrown out. The judge said that the decision was ‘not of any significance’. The decision was overturned on appeal.

The judge could refuse to entertain a cassation appeal if it considered that no significant legal issue arose in the case. It referred to the applicant’s objection in one sentence only: “The fact that the judge, who took part in the judgment against which the appeal was subsequently lodged, participated in a decision by which this appeal was found inadmissible is of no significance”. The judge ruled that the appeal had been ‘inadmissible’ and that ‘no significant issue’ had arisen. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that it was ‘unsubstantiated’ by the case law.

It referred to the applicant’s objection in one sentence only: “The fact that the judge, who took part in the judgment against which the cassation appeal was subsequently lodged, participated in a decision by which this appeal was found inadmissible is of no significance” The judge could refuse to entertain an appeal if it considered that no significant legal issue arose in the case or where there were no legal issues involved which would give rise to serious doubts or to discrepancies in case-law. The appeal was dismissed as ‘inadmissible’ by the judge on the basis that the case was not of ‘significant importance’.

The applicant claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against as his dismissal constituted less favourable treatment on racial grounds. He further argued that since the BNP was a ‘whites-only’ party, his dismissal also constituted indirect racial discrimination. The Employment Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not onracial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. On [DATE_TIME] he lodged a statutory claim of race discrimination in the Employment Tribunal pursuant to the Race Relations Act.

The Court of Appeal allowed Serco’s appeal and restored the order of the Employment Tribunal. Mummery LJ found the applicant's submission that he had been subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle and inconsistent with the purposes of the legislation. In rejecting the claim of indirect discrimination, the following was noted: “For indirect discrimination ... it is necessary to identify a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ which Serco has applied or would apply equally to persons not of the same race or colour’” The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people.

He was treated less favourably on the ground of a particular non-racial characteristic shared by him with a tiny proportion of the white population, that is membership of and standing for election for a political party like the BNP.

On [DATE_TIME] UNISON, the public sector workers’ trade union, sent a letter to Serco stating that many of its members found the applicant’s continued employment a ‘significant cause for concern, bearing in mind the BNP's overt and racist/fascist agenda’ 70-80 percent of Serco's customer base and 35 percent of its workforce were of [NRP] origin. UNISON asked that Serco take immediate action to ensure its members were not subjected to racial hatred. The applicant claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against as his dismissal constituted less favourable treatment on racial grounds. He lodged a statutory claim of race discrimination in the Employment Tribunal pursuant to the Race Relations Act. Serco had raised concerns that the applicant’s continued employment might lead to difficulties with other employees and damage its relationship with the unions. The Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. On [DATE_TIME] his appeal was upheld on the ground that the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase ‘on racial grounds’ by failing to interpret its meaning broadly. Serco was granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal. Mummery LJ found the applicant's submission that he had been subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle. The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people. The employment tribunal appears to have attempted itself a version of a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ in paragraph 5.6 of its decision (see paragraph 28 above). However, it is formulated too narrowly (membership of the BNP) to be meaningful. If such a provision were applied, however, it would not put persons of the same race as Mr [PERSON] ‘at a particular disadvantage’ when compared with other persons within section 1(1A) of the [DATE_TIME] Act. Court of Appeal ruled that Serco was not a public authority. Mr [PERSON] was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. He is not entitled to make a claim under it as Serco is not aPublic Authority’. “No case of indirect discrimination has been made out. As for justification under the [D date_time] Act I have already explained that it does not arise, as no case of indirectly discrimination has be made out,” the court added.

The case was transferred to the District Administrative Council for further investigations. The officer was taken into custody on suspicion of membership of the PKK. He confessed that he had been aiding and abetting the terrorists, providing them with food, clothes, weapons and medical equipment. The officers stated that [PERSON] had mentioned a shelter which was used.

No charges were brought against the man on account of his membership of the PKK on the ground that he had died on [DATE_TIME] The case was transferred to the District Administrative Council for further investigation. A major was appointed as a rapporteur to conduct further investigations into the killing of [PERSON]. The major took statements from the non-commissioned officers who had been on site during the incident. The officers stated that [Person] had been taken into custody on suspicion of membership of. the PKK and had confessed to aiding and abetting the terrorists.

Body of a man found dismembered in a PKK shelter in Bismil. Both legs of the man had been severed. Incident was reported to the police but no charges were brought against the man. He later confessed that he had been aiding and abetting the terrorists, providing them with food, clothes, weapons and medical equipment. He was released without charge on the grounds of lack of jurisdiction. The body was then handed over to a member of the village assembly for post-mortem examination. The Coroner ordered the PSNI to prepare a paginated and indexed bundle of all material held by them in relation to the death of [Person] in [DATE_TIME].
